DOCUMENT:
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Total | | £174,000" -- The cost lines sum to £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = £164,000, not £174,000. The growth bid is overstated by £10,000.
2. [inconsistency] at: "The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand" -- Section 3 states the Ashgrove pilot ran from October 2025 to March 2026, i.e. six months; the conclusion calls it a twelve-month pilot.
3. [misread_evidence] at: "Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level" -- Table 1 shows 21 visits per hour in the new weekday evening slot versus 46 and 58 in weekday daytime slots, i.e. less than half the daytime level. The text misstates the table, and the claim of strong evening demand rests on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

The proposal is well structured and the pilot is a real strength. However, there are several factual and arithmetic problems, and some go to the heart of the case. Several also appear in your own summary, so Members could be misled on points they are likely to check.

## Major issues

**1. The costs don't add up to £174,000.**
Table 2 gives £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000**, not £174,000. Either a £10,000 line is missing or the total is wrong. In a budget paper, finance colleagues will spot this immediately. It will undermine the "carefully costed" claim. Fix the total, or add and explain the missing item.

**2. Evening use is not "close to daytime levels".**
Table 1 shows evening visits at **21 per hour**, against 46 and 58 for weekday daytime slots. That is roughly 35–45% of daytime use, or under half. The sentence in Section 3 and the conclusion in Section 8 both contradict your own data. So does your summary. The evening slots are the weakest part of the pilot. Sunday, at 52 per hour, is the strong result.

Suggested approach: present evening use honestly as modest but meaningful. Lean on the job club, which was fully booked by week three, and on the 44% survey finding to justify it. You might also consider whether one late evening, plus Sunday, would give better value.

**3. The pilot lasted six months, not twelve.**
Section 3 says October 2025 to March 2026. Section 8 calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot". This matters because:
- Six months of winter data may not reflect summer patterns.
- Utilities were "scaled to a full year" from winter spend, so they are probably overstated. That is the conservative direction, but you should say so.

**4. Ashgrove's results are applied to all five branches.**
The ~84,000 visits figure (6 hrs × 21 + 4 hrs × 52 = 334 visits per week, × 50 weeks × 5 branches ≈ 83,500) assumes every branch performs like Ashgrove. Section 7 admits Ashgrove is your **busiest** branch and that other branches may see lower demand. The £2-per-visit figure therefore assumes the best case.

Section 3 also says the pilot "shows... the new hours will be well used across all five branches". One branch cannot show that. The same applies to the utilities cost, which is Ashgrove's figure applied to every branch regardless of size.

Suggested approach: give a range. For example, if the other four branches achieve 60% of Ashgrove's rate, roughly 61,000 visits at about £2.70 per visit. That is still below the £3.40 borough average and so still makes your case.

**5. The self-service alternative is not shown to cost more.**
Section 6 doesn't actually say self-service would cost more overall, but your summary does. On the paper's own figures:
- Self-service saves about two-thirds of £124,000 in staffing, roughly **£83,000 a year, every year**.
- Building works cost £60,000 × 5 = **£300,000, once**, and would be capital rather than revenue.

The works would pay back in about 3.6 years, after which self-service is cheaper. The stronger and more defensible argument is the one already in Section 6: self-service cannot deliver the staffed activities that drove the pilot's success. Lead with that, and drop the claim that it costs more.

## Moderate issues

- **Rise in memberships.** The increase from 690 to 1,140 (+65%, so "about two-thirds" is fair) is a simple year-on-year comparison. Other factors such as promotions, wider trends or the job club itself could contribute. Also, memberships are not split by time slot, so they don't show the *extended hours* drove the rise. Present this as supportive evidence, not proof.
- **Additional vs displaced visits.** Some evening and Sunday visitors may simply have moved from other times. "84,000 additional visits" should be qualified, or the pilot data should be checked for any change in daytime footfall.
- **Kiosk upgrades.** A self-service kiosk maintenance contract appears in the costs, yet self-service opening is rejected. Explain why it is needed for staffed hours.
- **50-week assumption.** Most bank holidays fall on Mondays, which are not extension days. Explain the basis, for example Christmas and Easter closures, or use a more accurate figure.
- **Single blended staff rate.** One rate including the Sunday enhancement is applied to all hours, including weekday evenings. This is not quite costing "from first principles". Splitting the evening and Sunday rates would be more transparent and might lower the cost.

## Minor points

- "Measured hour by hour" in your summary overstates Table 1, which gives averages by time slot.
- The recruitment risk relies on one branch's experience. Sunday working across five branches may be harder to staff.

## Summary of corrections needed before submission

| Issue | Location | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Total £174k vs items summing to £164k | Table 2, Sections 1 and 8 | Correct the total or add the missing line |
| "Evening close to daytime" | Sections 3 and 8 | Restate as about 40% of daytime; emphasise the job club |
| "Twelve-month pilot" | Section 8 | Change to six months |
| Ashgrove extrapolated to all branches | Sections 3 and 5 | Add a lower-demand scenario |
| Self-service "costs more" | Summary / Section 6 | Argue on service quality, not cost |

The underlying case is reasonable, especially for Sunday opening, and it survives honest correction. As written, though, the errors are the kind that make Members distrust the rest of the paper.
